quote: But the proverb does appear true to some degree, and I propose that we should be very disturbed by this fact.
content: On the empirical core, the essay is broadly right but for a reason that complicates its alarm. Intelligence and rationality are measurably separate constructs: performance on heuristics-and-biases tasks correlates only weakly with cognitive ability, and Stanovich has shown at length that thinking biases are largely independent of cognitive ability (Stanovich & West 2008). The bias blind spot can even increase with cognitive sophistication (West, Meserve & Stanovich 2012). That undercuts the framing that competence outside one's specialty "should" follow from competence inside it; rationality does not ride along with expertise, so finding the two decoupled is the expected result, not an alarming anomaly demanding that we "sit bolt upright."

The inference drawn here, that a religious scientist "literally doesn't know why you have to look at things," is far stronger than the evidence supports. Religiosity among working scientists is common rather than aberrant: surveys find a large minority believe in a personal God (Larson & Witham 1997; Ecklund's Science vs. Religion, 2010), even as belief drops sharply among elite National Academy members. Cognitive science treats "compartmentalization," holding domain-bounded models that are not reconciled with one another, as a near-universal feature of human cognition, not a diagnostic of failing to grasp experimentation. Going from "holds a religious belief" to "does not understand the purpose of empirical inquiry" skips over the well-documented fact that the two routinely coexist in the same competent practitioner.
